newsitem.title: USA: Golden Venture immigrants released from captivity.
newsitem.headline: Golden Venture immigrants released from captivity.

text.p: Thirty-nine Chinese immigrants imprisoned for more than 3-1/2 years after a smuggling ship ran aground off New York were released from confinement on Wednesday.

York County Prison warden Tom Hogan told Reuters the Golden Venture immigrants were released shortly after noon under authorization from federal immigration officials, who had been told by the White House to release them by March 1.

They were taken to an undisclosed location to meet local activists and sponsors in this conservative south-central Pennsylvania community, which has rallied around its unlikely guests and campaigned for their release.

The immigrants will live with their sponsors pending hearings in New York on asylum requests in which they contend they were fleeing restrictive "one-child" population policies in China or other forms of persecution.
"It went real smooth," Hogan said of the release. He described the immigrants as "model inmates" at the facility.

They were among the survivors of the wreck of the Golden Venture, a decrepit cargo ship that ran aground on June 3, 1993 off a beach in the New York borough of Queens. Ten of the 286 passengers drowned trying to swim ashore and some others escaped.
Of those who were captured, 99 were deported to China, others were released on asylum or sent to third countries and the rest were imprisoned for illegally entering the United States.

Fifteen of the Golden Venture immigrants in detention in Bakersfield, California, also are to be released under a White House decision this month. The White House said new laws to deter illegal immigration made it possible to release them.

In York, a broad group of community members had campaigned for release of the immigrant prisoners, holding weekly vigils outside the prison, helping with asylum applications and selling the prisoners' art to raise money for legal cases.

"I'm a very conservative Republican, certainly against illegal immigration," said one of the activists, 39-year old homemaker Cindy Lobach. "However, when someone is fleeing persecution, the U.S. has always been a haven. Someone fleeing should be granted asylum here, protection."

Said immigrant Chen Sherm Dee, as he was awaiting release from the prison, "I'm very grateful to them (the activists). They really helped us, and I want to thank all of them. They work real hard on my freedom."

The immigrants will still face a number of legal and cultural obstacles and possible retribution from organized crime figures who ran the smuggling operation, said the Rev. Joan Maruskin, a United Methodist minister from nearby Yoe, Pennsylvania.

"They know that the 'snakeheads' (smugglers) that brought them over will be looking for them. But they're not being set free with no assistance. We've worked hard to build a hospitable community for them," she said.
